title: The Subliminal Popcorn Hoax
objective: After this level you can explain what subliminal perception can and cannot do, and why the 1957 movie theater claim was made up.
summary: In 1957 James Vicary claimed hidden "Eat Popcorn" messages boosted cinema sales; he later admitted he made it up. Subliminal effects are real in the lab but small, and depend on what you already want.

cards.headline: In 1957, hidden words on a movie screen supposedly sold popcorn.
cards.body: Market researcher James Vicary claimed that briefly flashing "Eat Popcorn" during a movie, below conscious awareness, raised popcorn sales by more than 50 percent. If true, advertisers could steer you without your knowing. Was it true?

cards.headline: Below the threshold
cards.body: To be detected, a stimulus has to be strong enough. The absolute threshold is the minimum amount of stimulus energy you detect 50 percent of the time. A message below the threshold for conscious awareness is subliminal: you receive it, but you aren't aware of it. Vicary's claim was that subliminal words could change what people bought.

cards.headline: It never happened
cards.body: Vicary later admitted the study was made up. Nobody has ever replicated his findings. One of the most famous claims for subliminal persuasion was a hoax.

cards.headline: What hidden messages can do
cards.body: Lab research shows people can process and respond to information outside awareness. But hidden messages have little effect on behavior outside the lab. In a 2006 study, subliminally flashing the drink brand Lipton Ice increased choice of that brand, but only among participants who were already thirsty. It nudged a choice people were ready to make; it didn't create the thirst.
